title: Python Environment for Search and Graph Labs
content:
A [virtual environment](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/) keeps this workspace's packages separate from other Python projects. Use Python 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14, which are supported by the current [NetworkX release](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/install.html). PyCharm or VS Code can use the same environment as the terminal.

## Create the environment

Open a terminal in the folder where the search and graph labs will be saved. Check the selected Python version with `python3 --version` on macOS/Linux or `py -3 --version` on Windows. If several versions are installed, select a supported one before creating the environment.

On macOS or Linux:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

In Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
py -3 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

If activation is unavailable, use `.venv/bin/python` on macOS/Linux or `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` on Windows in place of `python` below. Activation changes which interpreter the terminal finds; the environment also works through its explicit interpreter path.

Install the graph, plotting and notebook tools:

```sh
python -m pip install networkx matplotlib jupyterlab
```

If a selected lab supplies `requirements.txt`, use `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` for its declared dependencies. Record the versions that work in this environment with `python -m pip freeze > requirements-local.txt`.

## Run a checkable example

Save the following as `check_environment.py`:

```python
import sys
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

graph = nx.path_graph(3)
print(sys.executable)
print(nx.shortest_path(graph, 0, 2))
nx.draw_networkx(graph, pos={node: (node, 0) for node in graph})
plt.axis("off")
plt.savefig("graph-check.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()
```

Run `python check_environment.py`. The first line should point inside `.venv`; the second should be `[0, 1, 2]`. Open `graph-check.png`: nodes 0, 1 and 2 should form a connected path. The `Agg` plotting backend saves the image without opening a desktop window. The [NetworkX tutorial](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/tutorial.html) explains the graph operations; the [Matplotlib guide](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html) explains figures and plotting.

## Keep the interpreter consistent

Select this same `.venv` interpreter in the editor. For notebook work, run `python -m jupyterlab` from the workspace folder, create a Python notebook, and check `import sys; print(sys.executable)` in its first cell. A different path means the notebook is using a different environment, which can explain imports working in the terminal but failing in the notebook. See [starting JupyterLab](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/starting.html) for the notebook interface.

Keep an experiment log beside the lab: the command used, the input graph or state, the expected result and the observed result. For this check, record the interpreter path, `[0, 1, 2]` and the generated image.


**Course flow:** Establish one reproducible graph-and-search workspace and a short experiment-log format. Refresh objects only when the state model shows a concrete prerequisite gap.

title: Bridge Positioning between Core Python and ML
content:
## State and decision systems

A search program chooses a sequence of allowed actions. Its inputs are an initial state, transition rules and a goal test. Its output can be a route and an explanation of the choices. A rule system applies conditions written by its author. A learned model instead fits behavior from examples.

For a delivery robot, a state might be its room; a move follows a doorway; the goal is a named destination. Breadth-first search can find a minimum-doorway route when every move has equal cost. If the battery level restricts movement, room alone is insufficient: the state must also record the remaining charge.

The Python prerequisites are functions, lists, dictionaries, sets and simple classes. A list can hold pending states; a dictionary can map a discovered state to its parent. Graph search, rules and game evaluation are the core of this course. Machine Learning develops fitting and evaluating learned models; Data Science in Python develops questions, data preparation and analysis. A search trace supports a claim about the supplied problem and rules, rather than a claim of general intelligence.

title: How to Read an AI Problem Statement
content:
## Specify a problem before searching

Use the directed graph `S: [A, B], A: [G], B: [], G: []`. The initial state is S. Legal actions follow listed arrows; the goal test is equality with G. Each action costs one. A valid solution is S,A,G, with two actions. Reaching B is a dead end, not success.

A state must contain everything needed to determine future legal actions and outcomes. Two visits to the same room with different keys may be different states. An action generator returns only legal successors; a goal test checks the complete requirement. Cost measures the route already taken, whereas a heuristic estimates work still remaining.

An output contract removes ambiguity: a found route includes start and goal; start=goal has a one-state route and zero actions; an unreachable goal has an empty route and no route cost. Invalid input and a valid problem with no solution are different outcomes. Record the neighbor order and tie rule when comparing traces. Several correct algorithms can find different routes with the same cost.

title: Experiment Logging and Reflection
content:

Repeat with goal S and with an isolated goal Z added as Z:[]. Keep the input graph, algorithm, neighbor order, expected route, observed route, action count and outcome in a short observation record. The ordinary route is S,A,G with two actions; start=goal has zero actions; Z is unreachable. Explain any mismatch using the first incorrect trace row. Record an unexecuted prediction as a prediction.

module: Unit 1: AI Landscape and State Representation
title: AI Landscape and State Representation Core Concepts
content:
## Represent states and transitions

A graph consists of states and connections between them. In a directed graph, S→A permits travel from S to A; it does not imply A→S. An adjacency dictionary represents the directed graph below. A state with no successors still appears with an empty list.

```python
graph = {"S": ["A", "B"], "A": ["G"], "B": [], "G": []}
```

## Worked route and state identity

The keys are stable state identifiers. The neighbor lists describe allowed transitions, in a reproducible order. S,A,G is a legal route; S,B,G is illegal because B has no edge to G. A route cost is the sum of its edge costs. In this unweighted example each transition costs one, so the route has cost two.

A Node object can hold an identifier and neighbors; a Graph object can look up nodes and add edges. Keep identifiers unique. Decide whether adding an edge creates a directed connection or two undirected connections, and implement that contract consistently. Check that both endpoint nodes exist before changing adjacency.

State equality is a modeling choice. For a locked-door problem, (room,has_key) distinguishes visits that allow different actions. A representation that keeps only room can discard a necessary return visit after obtaining a key.

A graph records possible transitions. The search frontier records which discovered states still need examination. Keeping those responsibilities separate allows BFS, DFS and cost-based searches to use the same problem model.

module: Unit 2: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition
title: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition Core Concepts
content:
## A frontier has an order

A stack removes its newest entry first: last in, first out. A queue removes its oldest entry first: first in, first out. Both can hold pending states, but they choose different next steps.

For a stack, `append` pushes and `pop()` removes the last list entry. For a queue, `collections.deque` supplies `append` and `popleft` without repeatedly shifting a list. An empty removal requires an explicit contract, such as a check before removal or a documented exception.

## Worked frontier trace

Start with S. Remove it and insert A then B. The stack next removes B; the queue next removes A. After a queue removes A and inserts C, its contents are [B,C], so B is next. This is the mechanism behind breadth-first exploration.

For DFS that should visit A before B, place B on the stack before A. State both the neighbor order and push order: saying only 'use a stack' does not determine the trace. A frontier entry can carry a state or an entire candidate route. The route representation makes a first experiment easier to inspect; a parent map avoids copying whole routes later.

The frontier may contain discovered states not yet expanded. A visited or discovered set prevents cycles from creating endless work. In BFS, marking on insertion ensures a state is queued once. A failed empty removal is a data-structure issue; finding no route after exhausting a valid frontier is a search outcome.

content:

title: Informed and Bounded Search Core Concepts
content:
## Limits, path costs and estimates

Depth counts edges from the start. Depth-limited search (DLS) explores at most a chosen depth. A goal exactly at the limit is accepted. A cutoff means a legal continuation was excluded by the limit; failure means all allowed cycle-free possibilities were exhausted. A cutoff alone does not prove a goal unreachable.

## Worked depth and cost cases

On S:[A,B], A:[C], C:[G], B:[], G:[], limits 0,1,2 produce cutoffs; limit 3 finds S,A,C,G. Iterative deepening repeats DLS at 0,1,2,3. It trades repeated shallow work for a small depth-first frontier. Track repeated states on the current path: a global closed set can incorrectly suppress a later shallower arrival.

For weighted paths, g(n) is accumulated route cost. Uniform-cost search orders by g. Greedy search orders by remaining-cost estimate h(n). A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n).

Use edges S-A=1, A-G=20, S-B=5, B-G=1 and estimates h(S)=0,h(A)=0,h(B)=1,h(G)=0. Greedy chooses S,A,G with cost 21. A* compares its cost 21 goal candidate with B's f=6, then finds S,B,G with cost 6. Low h alone does not account for an expensive incoming route.

For these finite examples use nonnegative finite costs. UCS stops when the cheapest queued goal is removed, rather than when any goal is first generated. A* additionally needs admissible estimates, h(goal)=0 and reopening after cheaper arrivals for its cheapest-path guarantee. An admissible estimate never exceeds the true cheapest remaining cost. Queue entries can become stale when a cheaper arrival is found; skip them.

title: Heuristics and Game AI Core Concepts
content:
## Evaluate a game tree

A game state includes the board and whose turn it is. Legal actions produce successor states. A terminal test stops expansion after a win or draw. Game-tree branches represent possible continuations, not promises about an opponent's actual move.

## Worked game positions

For Tic-Tac-Toe, number cells 0..8 in row-major order. X moves first. After two moves by each player, the board XX-/OO-/--- has X to move. Index2 wins immediately. On OO-/X--/-X-, X must block the top row at index 2 before considering a longer plan.

Choose a fixed scoring perspective. In the later O-agent studio, an O win scores +1, an X win -1 and a draw 0. At O turns maximize successor values; at X turns minimize them. The value of the empty board under complete optimal play is 0. Immediate win/block rules are a useful improvement over random choice, but fork positions show why they are not a complete strategy.

A heuristic estimates a nonterminal position when full expansion is too expensive. A minimax value from complete search is an exact outcome under the modeled rules and optimal future play. Neither is a probability of beating every human.

Create fresh child boards rather than mutating one board shared by siblings. Stop generating moves from terminal states, reject occupied cells and verify turn counts. Log each legal candidate and its score. A deterministic tie rule, such as lowest index, makes repeated comparisons reproducible.

title: Core Project: Heuristics and Game AI
content:
Use the linked tree-node example to inspect board state, turn, successors and terminal detection. Keep an untouched copy. Add an observation driver that prints legal move indices and child boards for XX-/OO-/--- and OO-/X--/-X-, both with X to move.

Confirm index 2 wins the first case and prevents O's immediate win in the second. A won or full board must offer no next moves. Changing one child must leave the original board and other children unchanged.

Add a lowest-index legal policy as a reproducible baseline. Record its selected move, then compare an immediate-win/block policy on the same two cases. Explain why two successful cases do not establish unbeatable play. Continue to the Tic-Tac-Toe studio for complete minimax, fork handling and its explicit O-centered scoring contract.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI Core Concepts
content:
## Features and evaluation

A feature is a measurable property of state: distance remaining, legal-move count or accumulated cost. A feature can help order choices, but it need not determine the goal. The blank can be in its goal cell while other puzzle tiles are wrong.

Evaluate against a stated contract. For search, record whether a valid route was returned, its edge cost, number of expanded states and whether the algorithm terminated. Separate invalid input from a valid unreachable problem. Compare algorithms on the same graphs, costs, neighbor order and stopping rule.

## Worked comparison

Use three solvable cases: the reference weighted graph has greedy cost 21 and A* cost 6; a single edge S-G=2 has cost 2 for both; start=goal has cost 0. Both solve 3/3, while mean route cost over those cases is 23/3 for greedy and 8/3 for A*. The success count hides the cost difference. Add a fourth valid case with an isolated G: both should report no route. Do not record that expected outcome as a discovered route.

A benchmark is a chosen collection of cases. Report per-case results and failure slices before a combined average. A set containing only direct edges cannot expose greedy's weighted detour. Timing also depends on machine and setup, so keep expansion counts and measurement conditions alongside elapsed time.

Responsible evaluation names affected people, a plausible failure and a response. A toy route planner that ignores stair access can return a mathematically short route that a traveler cannot use. Include accessibility in legal actions and allow a person to inspect or reject the proposed route. These toy fixtures establish behavior under their stated rules.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Labels, Benchmarks, and Success Criteria
content:
## Decide what counts as success

A reachable label answers whether a legal route exists; it does not identify the cheapest route. Check reachability independently on a tiny graph before evaluating a policy. A candidate route passes validity only when its endpoints match the request and every consecutive transition is legal.

For a minimum-cost task, compare the reported cost with the sum of actual edge costs and with a trusted small-case optimum. A program that returns a valid cost 21 route when a cost 6 route exists passes reachability and fails minimum-cost success. A fast timeout passes neither requirement.

Keep the number of cases visible in each measure. Solved/solvable is a different fraction from correctly handled/all cases. An intentionally unreachable graph belongs in the latter measure; excluding every failure from an average can make a weak policy look better. Report failures and exclusions beside the average.

title: Capstone and Portfolio Build Core Concepts
content:
## A capstone with a checkable baseline

The required starting scope is a 3×3 sliding 8-puzzle. Its board contains tiles 1..8 and one blank, each exactly once. A legal move swaps the blank with one orthogonal neighbor. The goal is `123/456/78_`, where _ denotes the blank. Every move costs one.

## Worked two-move puzzle

Use start `123/456/_78`. Moving tile 7 left gives `123/456/7_8`; moving 8 left reaches the goal. This is a two-move route. Count transitions, rather than displayed boards: three boards represent two moves.

BFS provides a minimum-move baseline. A* can use Manhattan distance: for each numbered tile, add its row and column displacement from its goal cell; exclude the blank. The example start has estimate 2. One move changes the distance of one numbered tile by one, so this estimate never exceeds the minimum remaining moves. A* must still track cheapest arrivals and skip stale queued entries.

A valid board can be unsolvable. On an odd-width 3×3 board, remove the blank and count inverted numbered-tile pairs. Odd parity cannot reach the ordered goal. The board `123/456/87_` has one inversion and must return an unsolvable result.

A finishable capstone preserves the working baseline, adds one justified comparison and supplies a reproducible report. Changing presentation alone does not establish an algorithmic improvement. Route legality, move count and unsolvable detection remain acceptance conditions when a visualizer is added.

title: Core Project: Capstone and Portfolio Build
content:
Run the linked completed 8-puzzle reference with python3 main.py and reproduce its two-move default. Create a separate capstone working copy and preserve the reference.

Record BFS and A* results for `123/456/_78`, the goal `123/456/78_`, and unsolvable `123/456/87_`. Expect two moves, zero moves and an explicit unsolvable outcome. Validate that each returned board uses every tile exactly once and each transition is one orthogonal blank swap.

Add one chosen valid board with at least four legal moves from the goal, recording how it was generated. Compare expanded states and returned move counts for BFS and Manhattan A* under the same limits. A scramble can immediately undo a move, so scramble length alone is not a shortest-distance label.

Deliver the board fixtures, reproducible commands, route validator, result table and a short explanation of the chosen improvement and limitations. If time or expansion limits stop a run, record an incomplete result rather than an invented route. Maze or marble-game alternatives retain the same baseline/comparison/report requirements with their own rules.

title: Build for Explanation, Not Just Output
content:
## Make the result inspectable

A puzzle report connects an initial board to a sequence of legal moves. Keep the initial board, each move, resulting board, goal check and total move count. A trace also records why the frontier selected the next state: queue order for BFS, or g,h and g+h for A*.

Use a result table with the same fields for both algorithms: case, outcome, valid route, moves, expanded states and limit. Keep the original raw output with the report. A summary that says 'A* is faster' needs matching inputs and measurements; a smaller expansion count on one board supports a claim about that board.

If the next project studies learned models, distinguish explicit search rules from fitted behavior. If it studies data analysis, distinguish the recorded algorithm observations from the questions asked of that data. The capstone's explanation should identify a justified next investigation from the observed results.

title: AI Level 1 Reference Guide
content:
## Search assumptions

A problem identifies state, legal actions, initial state, goal and cost. A frontier selects pending work; a discovered set and parent map record progress. On finite graphs, record cycle handling and tie rules alongside a trace.

BFS minimizes edge count when steps have equal cost. DFS is a reachability method and can return a longer route. UCS minimizes nonnegative finite route cost. A* orders by g+h; its cheapest-path contract requires an admissible estimate, h(goal)=0 and correct handling of cheaper arrivals. Greedy orders by h and does not generally minimize route cost.

Depth limits count edges. A goal at the limit is valid. A cutoff records an excluded continuation; it differs from exhausted failure.

References: [UC Berkeley uninformed search](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/search/uninformed.html) and [informed search](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/search/informed.html).

title: AI Level 1 Core Skills
content:
## Debug a state transition

Check representation before frontier policy. A missing key, incorrect turn or shared mutable board changes the problem even when the search loop is correct.

For a returned route, verify the initial state, goal and every legal edge. Recompute cost from the edges. For each parent link, confirm that the parent could generate the child. A visited-order list cannot replace these checks.

Compare the first differing trace row with a hand calculation. Inspect its selected state, pending frontier, cost and new discoveries. Copy mutable trace collections to preserve earlier snapshots. Change one condition at a time: neighbor order, edge cost, limit or heuristic.

For game search, state the player perspective and terminal utility. The maximizing and minimizing turns alternate under that fixed perspective. [UC Berkeley minimax](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/games/minimax.html) develops this rule.

title: AI Level 1 Next Topics
content:
## Extend a completed investigation

Keep a baseline case and its raw result before changing the problem. Transfer practice changes a state space or constraint; an extension adds a comparison or diagnostic. The eighteen optional project packs supply their own readings, fixtures and role files.

Choose a graph extension for reachability or cost, a puzzle extension for representation and heuristics, or a game extension for evaluation. Record the new input, prediction, actual result and reason for any difference. Preserve the original completion checks.

The optional reference bank contains completed demonstrations and earlier variants. Copy a completed example for an experiment, then implement and verify the assigned modification.

title: AI Level 1 Boundaries
content:
## Bound the claim

An algorithm's guarantee depends on its model and assumptions. A shortest walking route can be unsuitable when legal actions ignore stairs or closed doors. Identify those constraints before using a result to guide a decision.

Use fictional graphs, puzzles and game positions in these labs. A claim about learning from data requires an actual training process; these search and rule examples use authored transitions and scores.

A benchmark reports its cases, success contract, failures and limits. Keep timing conditions, random seeds and tie rules reproducible. A timed-out run remains incomplete. Human review can reject a result when important constraints are missing.

title: AI Level 1 Prerequisite Check
content:
## Python prerequisite check

The course uses functions, lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples and simple classes. A dictionary retrieves a state's neighbors; a set tracks discovery; a tuple can act as a stable board key. Lists and dictionaries are mutable, so copy snapshots that must retain an earlier state.

For a stack, use append then pop. For a queue, use collections.deque with append and popleft. A single item is removed first by either structure. Inserting A then B exposes the ordering difference.

Trace insert S, remove, insert A, insert B, remove, insert C, remove, remove. The stack returns S,B,C,A; the queue returns S,A,B,C. Check for empty before another removal or use a documented exception.

[Python deque documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.deque) describes these operations.

title: AI Level 1 Pathway Map
content:
## Choose a continuation

AI Level 1 develops explicit state, rules, search, heuristics and game evaluation. Machine Learning develops fitted models and their validation. Data Science in Python develops data questions, preparation, analysis and interpretation.

An algorithmic continuation can deepen search and proofs. A learned-model continuation can use meaningful state features as inputs with training and evaluation data. A data-focused continuation can analyze recorded experiments while retaining denominators and failure cases.

Keep a portfolio example with reproducible inputs, a working baseline, one justified improvement and an explanation of limits. That evidence identifies what is ready to build on and what needs further practice.

title: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants Core Concepts
content:
## Compare implementations

The reference bank provides optional graph, class, frontier and game demonstrations. The canonical Tic-Tac-Toe tree and its copy are different variants. The two marble-tree copies retain the same implementation; their filenames do not establish different learning outcomes.

The core studios evaluate reached Tic-Tac-Toe states with caching and marble positions from zero upward. Earlier tree examples eagerly construct future states. Compare initialization cost, repeated states, candidate scores and selected moves on the same legal positions. Keep each version's scoring perspective and terminal rule explicit.

Small stack, queue and class examples refresh prerequisites. The visualization examples use networkx and matplotlib in the local environment from the setup reading. To investigate an algorithm without graphics, use the supplied adjacency lists and search traces.
